title: Cornelius and Cyprian (16 September)
hook: a pope and a bishop, friends who disagreed and both died as martyrs

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy Name of Mary, the last word of Luke's sentence. Your line was Mary. Whose name did you say like it mattered? Day one thousand twenty-three.

A stack of letters, crossing the sea between two cities. One writer is Cornelius, bishop of Rome. The other writer is Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, in North Africa. They are writing in the aftermath of a persecution. Christians had been ordered to sacrifice to the Roman gods, and some gave in to save their lives. Now the pressure has eased, and those same people are at the church door, asking to come back in. What do you do with them? Two bishops had to answer that together, and they didn't always see it the same way. Today, two friends the Church keeps on one day.
screen: `TWO CITIES, A SEA, A STACK OF LETTERS.` → `THOSE WHO GAVE IN.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH THEM?`

segments.voice: The people at the door were called the lapsed: those who had fallen. Some in the Church said never. Once you deny Christ, the Church cannot take you back. A Roman priest named Novatian took that line so hard that he set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome. Others said the opposite: let them all back in, no questions. Cornelius chose a middle way. Welcome them home, after a time of penance. Mercy, but not pretending nothing happened. Now the friendship, which didn't start smoothly. When Cornelius was chosen, Cyprian held back at first, waiting to be sure the choice was sound. Then he backed him firmly, and wrote to him as a brother. On the lapsed, Cyprian had begun stricter, and he worked his way, with other bishops, to a path close to Cornelius's. Friends who disagreed, and kept writing. Cyprian wrote a whole treatise on the unity of the Church, with images like rays from one sun and branches from one tree. Paul's line in the Douay-Rheims could stand over both men: "Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Then both were taken. Cornelius was sent into exile and died there, and the Church honors him as a martyr. Cyprian was arrested later and tried. The account of his trial says that when the sentence of death was read, he answered with two words: Deo gratias. Thanks be to God. In the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass, the Roman Canon, their names are said side by side: Cornelius, Cyprian. Still together.
screen: `THE LAPSED AT THE DOOR.` · `MERCY, AFTER PENANCE.` · `A FRIENDSHIP THAT STARTED SLOWLY.` · `DEO GRATIAS.` · then, large: `THE UNITY OF THE SPIRIT IN THE BOND OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a letter in your head. Settle, and breathe. These two men kept their friendship going on paper, so choose someone whose views rub against yours, and begin, silently: Dear, and their name. First line: one thing in them you honestly respect. Their courage, their care for someone, their stubborn loyalty. Second line: one place you see it differently, said plainly, without heat. Then stop. No third line about who's right. Let the letter sit there, unsent. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well. The bell holds the time.

Lapsed, the word for those who had denied the faith under persecution and wanted back in. Cornelius and Cyprian, bishops of Rome and Carthage, disagreed on how to welcome them, and both died for the faith.
Your line: friends who disagreed. Today, say one honest good thing about someone you disagree with, to them or about them, and leave the argument for another day. Day one thousand twenty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saints Cornelius and Cyprian together on 16 September, and both names are said in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass.

fork.setup: you're a bishop after the persecution. people who sacrificed to the gods to save their lives are asking to come back. what do you do?
options: refuse them for good: they denied Christ.
welcome them back, after a time of penance.
let them all back at once, no questions.
fork.reveal: Cornelius took the middle way, and Cyprian came to stand close to him. Novatian refused them, and set himself up as a rival bishop.

original.note: Latin: thanks be to God. the account of Cyprian's trial gives it as his answer to the sentence of death.

trapdoor: what you thought: two old names in a list.
what it means: a pope and a bishop who worked through a hard question by letter, didn't always agree, stayed friends, and both died for the faith.
what a scholar hears: the question was the lapsed, Christians who sacrificed under persecution; Novatian refused them and set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome.

sources.quoted: Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

sources.ref: Cyprian, letters to Cornelius; On the Unity of the Church

notes: 'Friends who disagreed' (index): their documented differences were Cyprian's initial caution in recognizing Cornelius and his initially stricter line on the lapsed. Cyprian's sharpest dispute (over rebaptism) was with Pope Stephen, not Cornelius, and is not mentioned. Confirm the framing.
Claims rule: no dates (Decian persecution, 250; Cornelius d. 253 in exile at Centumcellae; Cyprian beheaded 258) and no numbers given.
The Roman Canon is called the first Eucharistic Prayer (its numbering in the Missal), avoiding the superlative 'oldest'.
Novatian 'set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome' (antipope). Confirm.
Cyprian's images of unity (rays of the sun, branches of a tree) are paraphrased from De Unitate 5. Confirm.
'Deo gratias' as Cyprian's reply to his sentence is from the Acta Proconsularia. Confirm.

Editor: hook no longer opens 'Two men...', which day 1015 (also two rivals in the Roman church) used; practice changed from bringing a rival to mind, a repeat of day 1015's practice, to a silent letter, drawing on the Cornelius-Cyprian correspondence.
